rv.q: Mr. Tucker’s production really ought to transfer to Broadway, where it would appeal to the same audience that kept “The 39 Steps” running for 771 profitable performances.
But this show, like “Sense and Sensibility,” is a gift to actors and a goody bag for its audience.
Please come and experience this spectacle known as Vanity Fair!
The direction, the acting, the tech elements all work in concert but above all it’s the canny script of Hamill that shines.

Written by Kate Hamill, whose earlier adaptation of Jane Austen's Sense and Sensibility made me a fan, Vanity Fair, also starring Hamill, is a show of great charm, with a sharpened feminist edge and a lively sense of contemporary relevance.
This Vanity Fair is a TKO putting a huge and seemingly unadaptable 19th century novel front and center on the stage of the Pearl Theatre.

Thackeray is another matter; the novelist's gimlet-eyed satiric view of an English society riddled with snobs, social climbers, and con artists proves highly amenable to Hamill and Tucker's theatrical treatment.

But more often than not, the hit-and-miss jokes let the air out of this colorful balloon of a show, and the second act becomes downright dour with its focus on war and on Hamill's message: "I was trying to play the game," Becky says to us.
Vanity Fair is the perfect blend of the world of Bedlam‘s theatrical inventiveness with the more classic Pearl Theatre Company.
The entire acting company deserves high praise for creating engaging, often deeply humorous, compelling characters.

The world premiere of Vanity Fair, Kate Hamill’s adaption of Thackeray’s satirical novel, as directed by Eric Tucker, is a great and glorious, equal parts cabaret, circus and non-judgmental morality play...
If the idea of reading Thackeray's 600+-page novel sounds impossibly daunting, you will be well served catching Hamill’s fresh, fast-paced, and wildly entertaining take.
Hamill and Tucker have invested this Vanity Fair with theatrical gusto, a sense of contemporary relevance, and a full measure of merriment.
The result is an eye-catching, attention-grabbing show that, although too long, lives up to Hamill’s conception with effectiveness.
Unfortunately, that's the one thing this production missed.
It’s ambitious, very ambitious. But it doesn’t live up to its ambitions.
The play is periodically entertaining, but chaotic (not freewheeling) in a style I find too often self-defeating.

Hamill follows up her inventive, extremely popular reimagining of Jane Austen's Sense & Sensibility with another creative marvel, a twenty-first-century take on William Makepeace Thackeray's 1848 novel Vanity Fair.
Thackeray's novel, no matter how approached, is simply "unstageable."

cn.t: Hamill's inventive adaptation and Tucker's playful direction energize Thackeray's classic with theatrical flair, though some find the clever staging gimmicks excessive and the production overlong. Critics praise the creativity but divide on depth.
